headline: AutoGen’s writable shell/filesystem plus AutoGPT’s filesystem/agent-protocol surface creates medium-risk prompt, leakage, and conflict pathways; compliance risk is low absent shared regulated data.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: AutoGen can read/write files and execute shell commands, and AutoGPT exposes filesystem and agent-protocol I/O. If AutoGPT writes attacker-controlled content into a shared workspace, AutoGen may ingest it as instructions. This is not provably blocked by either profile, but the shared-file pathway is configuration-dependent rather than default-safe.
conditions: IF both agents are pointed at the same writable directory
IF AutoGPT writes untrusted content that AutoGen later reads as task context
mitigations: Use separate working directories for each agent
Disable file-based handoff between agents
Add a human review step before AutoGen consumes AutoGPT outputs
requires-engineering: enforce provenance tags on shared files

B_data_leakage.rationale: AutoGen explicitly handles model-provider API keys and has broad network egress; AutoGPT can access the filesystem and agent protocol. If both share a workspace, sensitive application data touched by AutoGen can be exposed to AutoGPT outputs or downstream APIs. The profiles do not show PHI or secrets by default, so this is a workspace-mediated leakage risk rather than a guaranteed exfiltration path.
conditions: IF the same files contain secrets or sensitive application data
IF either agent forwards shared-file contents to its configured model/API backend
mitigations: Keep secrets out of shared directories
Mount read-only inputs for one agent and write-only outputs for the other
Rotate any exposed API keys immediately
requires-engineering: add content filtering before outbound requests

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Both agents can execute shell commands and spawn subprocesses, and both can write or access filesystems. AutoGen supports multiple instances with developer-defined shared state, while AutoGPT does not support multiple instances. That creates a realistic race/conflict pathway on shared mutable resources, though the profiles do not prove unrestricted same-dir writes or git mutation.
conditions: IF both agents operate on the same mutable filesystem tree
IF their shell actions overlap in time without external locking
mitigations: Assign disjoint directories per agent
Serialize write operations with a simple lock file
Avoid concurrent shell tasks on shared resources
requires-engineering: add orchestrator-level mutexes

D_cascading_error.rationale: AutoGen is a multi-agent orchestration framework that can emit tool-driven outputs, and AutoGPT can consume agent-protocol inputs. If AutoGPT treats AutoGen’s output as authoritative without verification, errors can cascade into downstream actions. The profiles do not show explicit verification or action authority, so this is a default-pathway concern rather than a guaranteed high-severity failure.
conditions: IF AutoGPT uses AutoGen output as task input without validation
IF downstream steps act on those outputs automatically
mitigations: Insert a validation step between agents
Require citations or checksums on transferred facts
Limit AutoGPT to read-only consumption of AutoGen outputs
requires-engineering: add schema validation for inter-agent messages

E_compliance.rationale: Both profiles are open-source and do not declare regulated-data handling, residency, or retention commitments. AutoGen handles model-provider API keys, while AutoGPT lists no secrets or special compliance scope. With no evidence of PHI, EU PII, or residency mismatch, the compliance risk is limited to documented gaps rather than a concrete breach pathway.
conditions: IF regulated data is introduced into either agent’s workspace
IF deployment policy requires residency or retention guarantees not provided here
mitigations: Keep regulated data out of the pair
Review vendor/data-processing terms before deployment
Log what data classes are allowed per agent
requires-engineering: enforce residency and retention controls
